questions.title: Two ways to add value, ranked in opposite orders
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 1: 1.1 What is a business? (the nature and role of business; adding value; the business functions). Toolkit: SWOT analysis and descriptive statistics.
questions.challenge_mechanism: Adding value is measured two defensible ways - per litre and per employee - and they rank the two options in opposite directions, while the mean customer spend is two and a half times the median, so the business's 'average customer' figure hides the concentration risk that a comfortable SWOT answer misses.

stimulus.title: Nettle & Vine
stimulus.body:
Nettle & Vine makes botanical cordial in a converted barn on the edge of the Lake District. Priya, a former food scientist, started the business nine years ago; her brother Tom, who had previously run a small group of cafes, joined two years later. The business employs six people and produces 60 000 litres a year at the single site, which now runs at full capacity on one shift. Tom handles sales and finance and Priya handles product development and production. Neither founder has a formal job title.

Almost all of the cordial is sold in 250 ml bottles to 40 independent cafes, delicatessens and farm shops within 100 miles of the barn. Every bottle carries the Nettle & Vine name, the founders' signatures and a short account of how the recipe was developed. Trade customers pay EUR 4.00 a litre. The bought-in materials and services - fruit, herbs, sugar, bottles, labels and the haulage that brings them in - cost EUR 1.20 a litre. Priya and Tom have never calculated how much value the business adds at each stage of production, and they have never worked out what a typical customer is worth to them.

Two of the six staff have been with the business since it began. The barn is leased from a local farmer on a rolling annual agreement. Priya sources most of her fruit and herbs from growers within the county and has twice refused cheaper imported alternatives, saying that the flavour and the story are the product.

The cordial market has changed since the business started. Supermarket own-label cordials now account for most of the volume sold in the country, and several independent producers have been bought by larger groups in the last three years. A rival producer 30 miles away, which also sells to independent retailers, was acquired by a national drinks company last spring and has since cut its trade prices. Tom believes Nettle & Vine will be squeezed out of its own market within five years if it stays the size it is.

A national supermarket chain has now approached Tom with an own-label contract. The supermarket would sell the cordial under its own brand, in its own bottle, at a price it would set. It wants 180 000 litres a year, delivered in weekly consignments, at EUR 1.55 a litre, for three years. The contract is exclusive: while it runs, Nettle & Vine could not sell its own branded cordial to any other retailer, so the existing trade business would end. The supermarket's own recipe would be used rather than Priya's, and the bottles would carry no Nettle & Vine branding. Deliveries would be steady, week by week, twelve months a year, and the supermarket would charge a penalty for any late delivery.

Because the site is at full capacity, the contract would need a new production line costing EUR 200 000, financed by a bank loan at 8% a year. The bought-in cost per litre would fall to EUR 0.40, because the supermarket would supply the fruit pulp in bulk at cost and would use its own low-cost packaging. Production would need eight staff rather than six. The bank has said that it will want personal guarantees from both founders before it lends.

The supermarket has told Tom that the EUR 1.55 price would be fixed for the first year and then reviewed annually. It has also asked for the right to visit the production site without notice and to change the specification of the cordial, within limits, without renegotiating the price. Other small suppliers to the same chain have complained publicly that their margins were cut at the first review.

The alternative - Option A - is to change nothing. Nettle & Vine keeps its own brand, its recipe, its 40 trade customers and its six staff. The founders know, however, that the business cannot grow on its current site, that a rival cordial maker has just been bought by a larger drinks group, and that two of their largest trade customers have asked for a lower price next year.

Priya and Tom each take a salary of EUR 26 000 a year, below what they could earn elsewhere, and the business has not paid a dividend in three years. All of the profit is reinvested. The trade customers value the cordial partly because it is not available in supermarkets; one cafe owner told Tom that the day he could buy it in a supermarket would be the day he stopped stocking it.

Priya is opposed to the contract. 'The moment our cordial goes into their bottle with their name on it, we are not a business any more, we are a factory. I did not spend nine years building a recipe for somebody else's label.' Tom disagrees. '180 000 litres at a stroke. We would be secure for three years, we would employ eight people instead of six, and I could finally pay myself properly. Sentiment does not repay a loan.' The two have not spoken to the supermarket since the first meeting, and Tom has not yet told Priya that the contract would require the trade accounts to be given up.

The table below shows the 40 trade accounts by annual spend.

table.caption: Nettle & Vine's 40 trade accounts by annual spend, year ended 31 March 2026.

questions.question: Priya and Tom must decide whether Nettle & Vine should accept the supermarket's exclusive own-label contract.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain **two** business functions at Nettle & Vine and how each function contributes to the value the business adds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the customer table, calculate the mean and the median annual spend per account. Then calculate value added, value added per litre and value added per employee for Option A and for the supermarket contract.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using SWOT analysis, evaluate whether Nettle & Vine should accept the supermarket contract. Refer to your calculations and to the objectives of the two founders.

questions.answer:
(a) Award up to four marks for two business functions, each explained in the context of Nettle & Vine.

Operations (production). The operations function is the transformation process: it converts bought-in inputs that cost EUR 1.20 a litre into bottled cordial that sells for EUR 4.00 a litre. Almost all of the value the business adds is created here, because the recipe, the brewing and the bottling turn cheap ingredients into a product a customer will pay a premium for. (A1)(A1)

Marketing. The marketing function is what allows the business to charge EUR 4.00 rather than a commodity price. The Nettle & Vine name, the founders' signatures, the story of the recipe and the refusal to use imported fruit are all marketing decisions, and they are the reason 40 independent retailers buy the cordial instead of a cheaper own-label alternative. Marketing therefore captures the value that operations creates. (A1)(A1)

Also creditable: finance (arranging and servicing the EUR 200 000 loan and costing the supermarket contract), human resources (recruiting and training the eight staff the contract would need), and product development (Priya's recipes and the product range).

(b) Customer data. Total annual spend of the 40 accounts is EUR 240 000, so the mean is $EUR 240 000 / 40 = EUR 6 000$. The median is EUR 2 400, because 25 of the 40 accounts spend only EUR 2 400 and the five largest spend EUR 20 000 each. (M1)(A1)

The mean is 2.5 times the median, so the 'average customer' is not a typical customer. The five largest accounts alone provide EUR 100 000, or 41.7% of trade revenue. The business is already more concentrated than the mean figure suggests. (A1)

Value added = revenue minus bought-in materials and services.

Option A: revenue $= 60 000 \times EUR 4.00 = EUR 240 000$; bought-in $= 60 000 \times EUR 1.20 = EUR 72 000$; value added $= EUR 168 000$. Value added per litre $= EUR 168 000 / 60 000 = EUR 2.80$. Value added per employee $= EUR 168 000 / 6 = EUR 28 000$. (M1)(A1)

Supermarket contract: revenue $= 180 000 \times EUR 1.55 = EUR 279 000$; bought-in $= 180 000 \times EUR 0.40 = EUR 72 000$; value added $= EUR 207 000$. Value added per litre $= EUR 207 000 / 180 000 = EUR 1.15$. Value added per employee $= EUR 207 000 / 8 = EUR 25 875$. (M1)(A1)

The two measures disagree. The contract adds more value in total (EUR 207 000 against EUR 168 000) and produces three times the volume, but it adds only EUR 1.15 a litre against EUR 2.80, a fall of 59%, and less value per employee. The contract buys volume with a much thinner margin.

(c) Indicative evaluation. A SWOT built from the case:

Strengths: a distinctive own brand; Priya's recipe; 40 loyal trade accounts; a premium price of EUR 4.00 a litre; a site that is full and profitable.
Weaknesses: no space to grow; no financial analysis; 42% of trade revenue from five accounts; only six staff; the founders' pay is low.
Opportunities: the supermarket contract would give three years of guaranteed volume; the craft drinks market is growing; a rival's takeover shows that small producers are attractive to larger buyers.
Threats: the contract is exclusive and would end the trade business; the brand would disappear from the bottles; the supermarket sets and reviews the price annually; a rival has cut its trade prices.

The quantitative case is closer than it first appears. The contract adds EUR 39 000 more value in total, but the EUR 200 000 loan costs EUR 16 000 a year in interest, so the gain falls to EUR 23 000, about 14% of Option A's value added. The supermarket may review the price after one year, and a cut of even 10% (to EUR 1.40) would reduce the contract's value added by EUR 18 000 and leave the business barely ahead of doing nothing while having given up its brand, its recipe and its independence. The loan also requires personal guarantees from both founders.

The SWOT shows that the contract removes the business's main weakness (no capacity to grow) by destroying its main strength (the brand). The descriptive statistics make the same point from the other direction: the business already depends on five large accounts, and the contract would replace that with dependence on a single customer that sets the price. Priya's objective is to protect the recipe and the identity of the business; Tom's is security and a proper income. The contract delivers Tom's objective only while the supermarket chooses to keep the price.

A supported conclusion is required. Rejecting the contract, or negotiating a non-exclusive, shorter or higher-priced deal, is creditworthy if the reasoning is consistent with the candidate's own figures. A conclusion that rests only on 'growth is good', or only on 'the brand matters', is not.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Two functions, two marks each: one mark for naming and describing the function correctly, one for explaining how it adds value in this business. 'Marketing' with no link to the EUR 4.00 price or the brand earns one mark only. Do not credit 'management' or 'administration' as a business function.

(b) Award (M1) for the mean and (A1) for the median; a candidate who computes the mean but not the median cannot reach the comment mark. The comment must identify that the mean is pulled up by the five large accounts - saying only 'the numbers are different' forfeits it. For value added, award (M1) for revenue minus bought-in costs and (A1) for each correct set of three figures; follow through on arithmetic slips. Accept value added per employee rounded to EUR 25 900 or EUR 26 000. Do not accept a candidate who puts the loan interest inside the value added calculation - interest is a financing cost, not a bought-in input - although such a candidate may still earn the evaluation marks in (c) if they use the figure there.

(c) The SWOT marks are for use, not for listing: a candidate who writes four headings and reaches no judgement earns at most two. The discriminating move is comparing the EUR 23 000 net gain with the scale of what is given up. Credit any supported conclusion. Do not credit generic statements about supermarkets or 'big business' that are not tied to the case.
questions.explanation:
The case is built so that the obvious answer - grow - is supported by the headline figures and contradicted by the analysis. The contract triples the volume, raises revenue from EUR 240 000 to EUR 279 000, and adds more value in total than Option A. Tom's case is not stupid, and the item is designed so that a candidate who simply says 'the supermarket is exploiting them' has not done the work.

The lever is that adding value can be measured in two defensible ways, and they point in opposite directions. Per litre, Option A adds EUR 2.80 and the contract adds EUR 1.15, a collapse of 59%: the contract converts a premium brand into a low-margin contract manufacturer. In total, the contract adds more (EUR 207 000 against EUR 168 000), because three times the volume of a thinner margin can still be more value. Neither measure is wrong, and the decision cannot be made without deciding which one the founders are trying to maximise - which is a question about the purpose of the business, not about the arithmetic.

The second layer is financing. The EUR 200 000 loan costs EUR 16 000 a year, which cuts the gain from EUR 39 000 to EUR 23 000. Because the supermarket may review the price after a year, a modest cut wipes that out. The commitment - personal guarantees, a three-year exclusive contract, the loss of the brand - is irreversible in a way the benefit is not.

The descriptive statistics are not decoration. The mean customer spend of EUR 6 000 is two and a half times the median of EUR 2 400, because five accounts dominate. That tells the student the business is already concentrated, so replacing 40 accounts with one is not a reduction in risk but an increase in it.

Classic wrong turns: comparing revenue rather than value added; treating the loan interest as a bought-in cost inside the value added calculation; praising the contract for creating two jobs without noticing that value added per employee falls; and answering (c) with a general discussion of supermarkets that never uses the figures.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Unit 1.1 bullet (the nature and role of business; adding value; the business functions), with SWOT and descriptive statistics as the two Toolkit tools. The scenario was constructed so that total value added and value added per litre rank the two options differently, so that the mean customer spend is 2.5 times the median, and so that the loan interest turns a EUR 39 000 gain into a EUR 23 000 one. The company, the contract terms, the customer table and every figure are original and were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Option A: 60000 x 4.00 = 240000; 60000 x 1.20 = 72000; value added 168000; per litre 2.80; per employee 28000. Contract: 180000 x 1.55 = 279000; 180000 x 0.40 = 72000; value added 207000; per litre 1.15; per employee 25875. Loan interest 200000 x 0.08 = 16000. Customer table sums to 240000 over 40 accounts; mean 6000; median 2400; top five accounts 100000 = 41.7% of revenue. Swept against the HL-only list: no 2.5 culture, 2.7 industrial relations, 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets, 4.3 forecasting, 4.6 international marketing or any 5.3/5.6-5.9 content; Toolkit tools used are SWOT and descriptive statistics only.

questions.title: A funding plan that balances on assumptions the bank has already refused
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 3: 3.1 Introduction to finance (the role of the finance function; why businesses need finance; capital and revenue expenditure). Toolkit: business plan.
questions.challenge_mechanism: The funding plan balances on its own assumptions but two of those assumptions are already contradicted by the case, so the visible capital items conceal a working-capital shortfall that the bank will not lend against, and the lease alternative shrinks the upfront gap only by enlarging the recurring one.

stimulus.title: Wagtail & Co
stimulus.body:
Wagtail & Co is a dog daycare and grooming business that Nia and Rob, two former veterinary nurses, plan to open in a converted unit on an industrial estate. Neither has run a business before, and they are preparing the financial section of a business plan in order to raise the money they need.

The unit needs converting before it can open. The conversion, including kennels, flooring, fencing and a secure outdoor yard, will cost EUR 52 000. Grooming equipment - tables, dryers, clippers and a hydrobath - will cost EUR 16 000. A van for collecting and returning dogs will cost EUR 28 000. Booking and payment software will cost EUR 6 000, and signage and the fit-out of the reception area will cost EUR 8 000. Nia and Rob have written quotations for all five items and believe the figures to be accurate.

The business will also have to meet running costs every month. Rent is EUR 3 000, wages for two full-time and two part-time staff are EUR 7 800, utilities are EUR 1 200, insurance is EUR 400, dog food and consumables are EUR 4 600, and marketing is EUR 500. These costs will start as soon as the lease is signed.

Nia and Rob expect the unit to take two months to convert and the staff to need two months of training, so the business will receive no income at all until the start of the third month. Their business plan therefore sets aside three months of running costs as working capital, and adds a contingency of 10% of the total of the capital items and the working capital.

The plan assumes the money will come from three places. Nia and Rob will put in EUR 45 000 of their own savings. They have asked the bank for a loan of EUR 115 000. They expect to receive a government start-up grant of EUR 20 000, which they have seen advertised. On that basis the plan shows total funding of EUR 180 000.

Two things have since changed. The bank has replied that it lends to start-ups only against assets, and will advance at most 60% of the value of the capital items in the plan. The grant body has confirmed in writing that the maximum award under the scheme is EUR 12 000. Rob's aunt has offered to provide the difference, but she wants 25% of the business in return, and both founders have said they do not want to give up any ownership.

A supplier has also offered to lease the grooming equipment and the van, which together cost EUR 44 000, for EUR 980 a month, instead of selling them outright.

table.caption: One-off items quoted by suppliers for the new unit.

questions.question: Nia and Rob must decide whether the funding plan in their business plan is realistic enough to open Wagtail & Co.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure, using examples from the case, and explain why the distinction matters when a start-up is deciding how much finance it needs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total finance required at start-up, showing the capital expenditure, the working capital requirement and the contingency separately.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the financial section of the business plan, evaluate whether the funding plan is realistic, referring to the bank's lending limit, the grant, the lease offer and Rob's aunt's proposal.

questions.answer:
(a) Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that will be used in the business for more than a year - it buys something the business keeps. Revenue expenditure is spending on the day-to-day running of the business, which is consumed within the year. (A1)(A1)

In this case the five items in the table are all capital expenditure: the conversion of the unit, the grooming equipment, the van, the software and the signage are assets the business will use for several years. The rent, wages, utilities, insurance, dog food and marketing are revenue expenditure, because they are incurred month by month and create no lasting asset. (A1)

The distinction matters because the two types of spending have to be financed differently. Capital expenditure is a large, one-off sum that a bank will often lend against, because the asset can be secured. Revenue expenditure recurs every month, is not secured by an asset, and must be financed from cash or from working capital - so it is easy to underestimate and hard to borrow against. (A1)

(b) Capital expenditure $= EUR 52 000 + EUR 16 000 + EUR 28 000 + EUR 6 000 + EUR 8 000 = EUR 110 000$. (M1)(A1)

Monthly running costs $= EUR 3 000 + EUR 7 800 + EUR 1 200 + EUR 400 + EUR 4 600 + EUR 500 = EUR 17 500$. Three months of running costs must be financed before the business earns anything, so working capital $= 3 \times EUR 17 500 = EUR 52 500$. (M1)(A1)

Contingency $= 10\% \times (EUR 110 000 + EUR 52 500) = 10\% \times EUR 162 500 = EUR 16 250$. Total finance required $= EUR 110 000 + EUR 52 500 + EUR 16 250 = EUR 178 750$. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation, using the financial section of the business plan.

The plan looks balanced on its own assumptions: it claims EUR 180 000 of funding against a requirement of EUR 178 750, a margin of EUR 1 250. But two of the three funding assumptions are wrong.

The bank will lend at most 60% of the value of the capital items, which is $60\% \times EUR 110 000 = EUR 66 000$, not the EUR 115 000 requested. The grant is capped at EUR 12 000, not EUR 20 000. The realistic funding is therefore $EUR 45 000 + EUR 66 000 + EUR 12 000 = EUR 123 000$, against a requirement of EUR 178 750. The shortfall is EUR 55 750, and the plan's apparent EUR 1 250 surplus becomes a EUR 55 750 hole. (M1)(A1)

The shortfall is almost entirely a working-capital problem. The business needs EUR 52 500 of cash to survive three months with no income, and the bank will not lend against it. The founders have focused on the visible assets and underestimated the cost of simply keeping the doors open.

The lease offer helps the capital side but not enough. Leasing the grooming equipment and the van (EUR 44 000) would cut capital expenditure to EUR 66 000, but it adds EUR 980 a month to running costs, raising monthly costs to EUR 18 480 and working capital to EUR 55 440. With a 10% contingency on EUR 121 440, the total requirement becomes EUR 133 584. The bank's limit then falls to EUR 39 600, so available funding is EUR 96 600 and the shortfall is EUR 36 984. Leasing reduces the gap by about EUR 19 000 but increases the monthly cost permanently.

Rob's aunt's EUR 56 000 would close the gap, but it costs 25% of the business, which both founders have said they do not want to give up. It also transfers a quarter of any future growth to someone who is contributing money rather than work.

A supported conclusion is required. A candidate who recommends delaying the opening, phasing the spend, reducing the contingency, or accepting the aunt's money, and who justifies it with the figures, should be credited. The key judgement is that the plan is not realistic as written: it understates the finance needed by about EUR 55 750 and misunderstands how a bank lends to a start-up.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Two marks for the distinction, one for applying it correctly to the case, one for explaining why it affects the finance decision. A candidate who says only 'capital is long term, revenue is short term' earns one mark. Do not credit an answer that classifies the monthly rent as capital because it is paid under a lease.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the capital total, (M1)(A1) for the monthly running cost and the three-month working capital, and (A1) for the contingency and the total. Follow through on arithmetic errors. Do not penalise a candidate who presents the contingency as 10% of capital plus working capital in a different order. Do not accept a total that omits the working capital: that omission is the whole point of the question.

(c) The two discriminating marks are for the bank's 60% limit and the grant cap. A candidate who accepts the plan's EUR 180 000 at face value and concludes that it is adequate cannot earn more than one mark, however well written. The lease marks require the candidate to see that leasing reduces the upfront requirement but raises the recurring one - a candidate who says only 'leasing is cheaper' forfeits them. Credit any supported conclusion, including one that keeps the plan but changes its funding. Do not credit answers that drift into evaluating the business idea itself rather than the finance plan.
questions.explanation:
The question is designed so that the plan appears to work. EUR 180 000 of funding against a requirement of EUR 178 750 is a surplus of EUR 1 250, and a candidate who checks only the addition will conclude that the plan is sound. The trap is that the funding side contains assumptions the case has already contradicted: the bank's lending rule and the grant cap are stated plainly, and both reduce the money actually available.

The deeper point, and the reason the item sits in Unit 3.1 rather than in sources of finance, is the difference between capital and revenue expenditure and what it means for how much finance a start-up actually needs. The visible, exciting items - the conversion, the van, the equipment - are the ones founders plan for. The invisible item is working capital: EUR 52 500 of rent, wages, insurance and consumables that must be paid for three months before the business earns a penny. Banks will lend against a van; they will not lend against next quarter's wages. So the shortfall is concentrated precisely where borrowing is hardest.

The lease option is a genuine second lever. Converting EUR 44 000 of capital expenditure into a monthly payment reduces the upfront requirement from EUR 178 750 to EUR 133 584 and cuts the shortfall from EUR 55 750 to EUR 36 984 - but it raises the monthly running cost and therefore the working capital requirement too. Students who treat leasing as a pure saving have missed the interaction between the two.

Classic wrong turns: adding only the capital items and reporting EUR 110 000 as the finance required; accepting the EUR 115 000 loan; forgetting the contingency; and concluding that the aunt's offer solves everything without noticing that it costs a quarter of the business, which the founders have said they will not give up.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Unit 3.1 bullet (role of the finance function; why businesses need finance; capital and revenue expenditure), with the business plan as the Toolkit tool. The scenario was constructed so that the funding plan balances on its face while two stated constraints (the bank's 60% asset limit and the grant cap) leave a EUR 55 750 shortfall, and so that leasing trades a smaller upfront gap for a larger recurring cost. The company, quotations, running costs and funding plan are original and every figure was recomputed.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Capital expenditure 52000 + 16000 + 28000 + 6000 + 8000 = 110000. Monthly running costs 3000 + 7800 + 1200 + 400 + 4600 + 500 = 17500; working capital 3 x 17500 = 52500; contingency 0.10 x 162500 = 16250; total 178750. Planned funding 45000 + 115000 + 20000 = 180000. Bank limit 0.60 x 110000 = 66000; grant 12000; available 123000; shortfall 55750. Lease case: capital 66000; monthly 18480; working capital 55440; contingency 12144; total 133584; bank limit 39600; available 96600; shortfall 36984. Swept against the HL-only list: no 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets or any other HL-only content; Toolkit tool used is the business plan only.

questions.title: A twenty per cent productivity gain that makes each garment worth less
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.1 The role of operations management (the transformation process; adding value through operations; efficiency and effectiveness). Toolkit: descriptive statistics.
questions.challenge_mechanism: Efficiency and effectiveness move in opposite directions: labour productivity rises by 20% while value added per garment falls, and the annual mean defect rate conceals a step change from about 2% to about 7% at the moment the process was altered.

stimulus.title: Pennine Workwear
stimulus.body:
Pennine Workwear makes protective clothing for construction and agricultural customers at a single factory in Lancashire. The company employs 64 people, of whom 40 work on the production line. It makes about 120 000 garments a year, and its order book is full for the next eighteen months.

Six months ago the operations manager introduced a new production process. The number of quality checks was halved, the line speed was increased, and the final inspection stage was combined with packing. The operations manager's bonus depends on labour productivity, measured as garments produced per direct labour hour, and he has reported a 20% improvement since the change.

The finance director has collected the following figures for a typical month before the change and a typical month since it.

Before the change: output 12 000 garments; direct labour hours 2 400; selling price EUR 18 per garment; bought-in materials EUR 7 per garment; defect rate 2%; cost of reworking a defective garment EUR 4.

Since the change: output 15 000 garments; direct labour hours 2 500; selling price EUR 18 per garment; bought-in materials EUR 7 per garment; defect rate 7%; cost of reworking a defective garment EUR 4; and 3% of output is now sold as seconds at EUR 9 instead of EUR 18.

The quality manager has also recorded the monthly defect rate for the past twelve months. The change was introduced at the end of month 6. Those figures are in the table below.

Two of Pennine's largest customers, who together account for about 30% of sales, have written to complain about the quality of recent deliveries, and one has asked for a meeting. Three experienced machinists have left in the past four months. The operations manager has asked the board to approve a further increase in line speed, arguing that the productivity gain has already been proved.

table.caption: Monthly defect rate, months 1 to 12. The new process was introduced at the end of month 6.

questions.question: The board of Pennine Workwear must decide whether to keep the new production process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the transformation process, how the operations function at Pennine Workwear adds value to the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the labour productivity and the value added per garment in a typical month before the change and in a typical month since the change. Comment on what your figures show.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using descriptive statistics on the defect-rate data, evaluate whether Pennine Workwear should keep the new production process.

questions.answer:
(a) Pennine Workwear operates a transformation process. The inputs are bought-in fabric, thread and components costing EUR 7 a garment, together with 2 400 hours of direct labour a month and the use of the factory and machinery. The process is cutting, sewing, finishing, inspecting and packing. The outputs are finished protective garments sold at EUR 18 each, which for many customers must also be safe, durable and compliant with industry standards.

The operations function adds value in two ways. First, it converts EUR 7 of materials into a garment that sells for EUR 18 - the transformation itself is where the added value is created. Second, it is responsible for the quality and reliability that make the garment worth buying: a protective jacket that fails in use is worthless, so the inspection and finishing stages protect the price the business can charge. Operations therefore supports the whole business strategy, not just the production line.

(b) Labour productivity = garments produced per direct labour hour.

Before the change: $12 000 / 2 400 = 5.0$ garments per labour hour. (M1)(A1)
Since the change: $15 000 / 2 500 = 6.0$ garments per labour hour. (A1)
That is a rise of $(6.0 - 5.0) / 5.0 = 20\%$, which is the figure the operations manager is reporting.

Value added = revenue minus bought-in materials minus rework cost.

Before the change: revenue $= 12 000 \times EUR 18 = EUR 216 000$; materials $= 12 000 \times EUR 7 = EUR 84 000$; defects $= 2\% \times 12 000 = 240$ garments, rework $= 240 \times EUR 4 = EUR 960$. Value added $= EUR 216 000 - EUR 84 000 - EUR 960 = EUR 131 040$, or $EUR 131 040 / 12 000 = EUR 10.92$ per garment. (M1)(A1)

Since the change: revenue $= 15 000 \times EUR 18 = EUR 270 000$, less 450 garments sold as seconds at EUR 9 instead of EUR 18, a loss of $450 \times EUR 9 = EUR 4 050$, so EUR 265 950; materials $= 15 000 \times EUR 7 = EUR 105 000$; defects $= 7\% \times 15 000 = 1 050$ garments, rework $= 1 050 \times EUR 4 = EUR 4 200$. Value added $= EUR 265 950 - EUR 105 000 - EUR 4 200 = EUR 156 750$, or $EUR 156 750 / 15 000 = EUR 10.45$ per garment. (M1)(A1)

The two measures disagree. Labour productivity is up 20%, but value added per garment has fallen from EUR 10.92 to EUR 10.45, a fall of about 4.3%. Total value added has risen, from EUR 131 040 to EUR 156 750, but only because 25% more garments are being made. Each garment now adds less value than before, because the cost of rework and of selling seconds has risen faster than the extra output is worth. Efficiency has improved; effectiveness has not.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics on the twelve monthly defect rates.

The mean defect rate for the year is $(2.1 + 1.8 + 2.3 + 1.9 + 2.2 + 2.1 + 6.8 + 7.1 + 6.4 + 7.6 + 8.1 + 7.4) / 12 = 55.8 / 12 = 4.65\%$. Taken alone, that looks acceptable. The median is 4.35% and the range is $8.1 - 1.8 = 6.3$ percentage points. (M1)(A1)

The mean is misleading. Splitting the data at the change gives a mean of 2.07% for months 1 to 6 and 7.23% for months 7 to 12. The process did not drift; it stepped from about 2% to about 7% at the moment the change was introduced, and the annual mean of 4.65% describes no month that actually occurred. This is the classic trap of a summary statistic that conceals a structural break.

Two of the largest customers, together worth about 30% of sales, have complained, and one has asked for a meeting. Three experienced machinists have left in four months, which will put further pressure on quality. The operations manager's bonus depends on productivity, which explains why he is recommending a further increase in line speed, but his measure ignores the cost of defects and returns.

Conclusion: the change should not be kept in its present form. The productivity gain is real, but it has been bought by cutting the quality checks that protect the EUR 18 price. A supported conclusion is required; a candidate who recommends keeping the change but restoring the inspection stage, and justifies this from the figures, is equally creditworthy.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Two marks for a correct description of inputs, process and outputs, and two for explaining how operations adds value. A candidate who describes the process without linking it to value added earns at most two. Do not credit a list of departments with no explanation.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the two productivity figures and (A1)(A1) for the two value added per garment figures. The comment mark is the discriminating one and requires the candidate to notice that productivity and value added per unit move in opposite directions. A candidate who reports only the productivity improvement, or who says 'both improved because total value added rose', forfeits the comment mark. Follow through on arithmetic slips. Accept value added calculated without the rework cost only if the same treatment is applied to both periods; a candidate who includes rework in one period and not the other cannot reach full marks.

(c) The descriptive statistics marks are for computing the mean, the median and the range, and for noticing that the annual mean conceals the step change. A candidate who reports only the mean of 4.65% and concludes that quality is acceptable has not used the data. The evaluation must end in a decision; credit either conclusion provided it is supported. Do not credit an answer that attributes the defects to staff attitudes without evidence.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the difference between efficiency and effectiveness, which is the heart of Unit 5.1. Efficiency asks whether the business is doing things right - more output per hour, lower unit cost. Effectiveness asks whether it is doing the right things - making something the customer will pay for and keep buying. The operations manager has improved the first and damaged the second, and his bonus is tied to the measure that improved.

The arithmetic is deliberately arranged so that the trap is visible but easy to miss. Labour productivity rises by exactly 20%, which is the figure the case quotes, and total value added also rises, from EUR 131 040 to EUR 156 750. A student who checks only these two numbers concludes that the change is a success. The figure that contradicts them is value added per garment, which falls from EUR 10.92 to EUR 10.45 because the cost of rework and of selling seconds rises faster than the extra output is worth. Twenty-five per cent more garments are being made, and each one is worth slightly less.

The descriptive statistics add a second, sharper point. The annual mean defect rate of 4.65% looks unremarkable, but no month had a defect rate near it: the process ran at about 2% and then stepped to about 7%. A summary statistic that averages across a structural break describes nothing real. This is why the question supplies twelve monthly figures rather than two averages, and it is what separates a candidate who can calculate a mean from one who can interpret it.

The qualitative evidence - two large customers complaining, three machinists leaving, a bonus tied to the wrong measure - is there to support the evaluation rather than to replace it. The strongest answers notice that the operations manager's incentive and the company's interest have diverged, which is why the recommendation is not simply 'work harder on quality' but 'restore the check that the change removed'.

Classic wrong turns: treating a 20% productivity gain as automatically good; using total value added instead of value added per unit; and reporting the annual mean defect rate without splitting it at the change.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Unit 5.1 bullet (the transformation process; adding value through operations; efficiency and effectiveness), with descriptive statistics as the Toolkit tool. The case was constructed so that labour productivity rises by 20% while value added per garment falls by about 4.3%, and so that the twelve monthly defect rates step from about 2% to about 7% at the point of the change, making the annual mean an unrepresentative statistic. The company, the process change and every figure are original and were recomputed.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Productivity 12000/2400 = 5.0 and 15000/2500 = 6.0, a 20% rise. Before: revenue 216000, materials 84000, defects 240, rework 960, value added 131040, 10.92 per garment. After: revenue 15000 x 18 minus 450 x 9 = 265950, materials 105000, defects 1050, rework 4200, value added 156750, 10.45 per garment (a fall of about 4.3%). Defect rates: months 1-6 mean 2.0667%, months 7-12 mean 7.2333%, annual mean 4.65%, median 4.35%, range 6.3 points. questions.title: A flow line that is cheaper per bench and dearer per year
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (job, batch and flow production; capital and labour intensity; factors influencing the choice of method). Toolkit: descriptive statistics and decision trees.
questions.challenge_mechanism: The choice of operations method is set by the volume per production run rather than the annual average volume: the flow line is cheaper per bench at the annual volume, but seasonal demand forces a pre-build whose storage cost is nearly twice the saving, so the method that looks cheapest is the one that costs most.

stimulus.title: Hartswood Garden Furniture
stimulus.body:
Hartswood Garden Furniture makes wooden garden benches, tables and chairs at a workshop in Somerset. It produces 120 000 units a year across twelve product variants and sells them through garden centres and a mail-order catalogue. All of the products are currently made by batch production.

The best-selling product is a two-seat bench, which accounts for 48 000 units of the annual output. Sales of the bench are highly seasonal: 80% of the annual volume is sold in April, May and June, and the remaining 20% is spread evenly over the other nine months. The company's marketing manager estimates a 0.6 probability that annual bench sales will be 48 000 units next year and a 0.4 probability that they will be 30 000 units, depending on the weather.

A consultant has proposed that Hartswood install a flow production line for the bench. Under the present batch system the bench has annual fixed costs of EUR 180 000 and a variable cost of EUR 18.25 a unit. The proposed flow line would have annual fixed costs of EUR 480 000 and a variable cost of EUR 10 a unit, and would cost EUR 600 000 to install. It would have a capacity of 8 000 benches a month. It could make only the bench; the other eleven products would stay on batch production.

Because the flow line cannot be expanded, any output needed above 8 000 benches in a month would have to be made in advance and stored. Hartswood's warehouse can hold the finished benches, but storing them costs EUR 3 per bench per month, and the consultant expects benches to be held for an average of four months. The finance director has also pointed out that a flow line is difficult to change over, so any design change to the bench would be expensive and slow.

questions.question: Hartswood Garden Furniture must decide whether to invest EUR 600 000 in a flow production line for its best-selling bench.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain **two** reasons why the consultant believes flow production would be suitable for the bench, and **one** reason why the company's other eleven products make flow production difficult.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean monthly demand for the bench and the demand in a peak month. Calculate the unit cost of the bench under batch production and under flow production at an annual volume of 48 000 units, and comment on the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using descriptive statistics and a decision tree, evaluate whether Hartswood should invest in the flow production line. Justify your answer with reference to capacity, storage cost and the product range.

questions.answer:
(a) The consultant's case for flow production rests on volume and cost. The bench is a single, standardised product made in large numbers - 48 000 units a year - and flow production is designed for exactly this: a continuous sequence of operations with little or no changeover, which spreads a high fixed cost over a large output and gives a low variable cost. Second, demand for the bench is predictable in total, and the consultant argues that a dedicated line would remove the batch changeovers that currently interrupt production. (A1)(A1)

The eleven other products are the problem. Flow production is only economic when a line can run for long periods without being stopped and altered. Hartswood makes twelve variants in total, and a flow line for the bench cannot make tables, chairs or the other bench designs. Those products must stay on batch production, so the investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while leaving the rest of the factory unchanged. (A1)(A1)

(b) Mean monthly demand $= 48 000 / 12 = 4 000$ benches. (A1)

Peak demand: 80% of 48 000 $= 38 400$ benches are sold in three months, so peak monthly demand $= 38 400 / 3 = 12 800$ benches. (M1)(A1)

Unit cost at 48 000 units:

Batch: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 180 000 / 48 000 = EUR 3.75$; plus variable cost EUR 18.25, giving EUR 22.00 per bench. (M1)(A1)
Flow: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 480 000 / 48 000 = EUR 10.00$; plus variable cost EUR 10.00, giving EUR 20.00 per bench. (A1)

Comment: at 48 000 units flow production is EUR 2.00 a bench cheaper, a saving of EUR 96 000 a year, and the crossover point at which flow becomes cheaper is $(EUR 480 000 - EUR 180 000) / (EUR 18.25 - EUR 10.00) = 36 364$ benches. Since annual demand is 48 000, the arithmetic appears to favour flow - but this comparison ignores the constraint that the flow line's capacity of 8 000 benches a month imposes on a seasonal product.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics and a decision tree.

The descriptive statistics show why the annual average is the wrong basis for the decision. Mean monthly demand is 4 000 benches, but peak monthly demand is 12 800 and off-season demand is about 1 067. The range is therefore about 11 733 benches a month. The flow line can make only 8 000 a month, so in each of the three peak months it is short by $12 800 - 8 000 = 4 800$ benches. Over the three months the shortfall is 14 400 benches, all of which must be made in advance and stored. (M1)(A1)

Storage costs EUR 3 a bench a month, and the consultant expects an average holding period of four months: $14 400 \times EUR 3 \times 4 = EUR 172 800$ a year. The EUR 96 000 saving from flow production is therefore more than wiped out, leaving flow production EUR 76 800 a year more expensive than batch at the higher demand level. (A1)

The decision tree makes the same point under uncertainty. Marketing estimates a 0.6 probability that demand is 48 000 and a 0.4 probability that it is 30 000.

Batch production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 18.25 \times 48 000 = EUR 1 056 000$; at 30 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 547 500 = EUR 727 500$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 056 000 + 0.4 \times EUR 727 500 = EUR 924 600$. (M1)(A1)

Flow production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 10 \times 48 000 = EUR 960 000$, plus storage of EUR 172 800, giving EUR 1 132 800. At 30 000, peak monthly demand is $0.8 \times 30 000 / 3 = 8 000$, which exactly equals the line's capacity, so no storage is needed and cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 300 000 = EUR 780 000$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 132 800 + 0.4 \times EUR 780 000 = EUR 991 680$. (M1)(A1)

Batch production has the lower expected cost, by EUR 67 080, and the conclusion does not depend on the probabilities: flow is more expensive in the high-demand state and also more expensive in the low-demand state, so no plausible weighting reverses it.

The flow line would also commit EUR 600 000, would be difficult to change over, and could not make the other eleven products. Conclusion: Hartswood should not invest in the flow line. A stronger answer will note that the same analysis would justify revisiting flow production if the company could smooth demand, reduce the product range, or add a second line to raise peak capacity.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Two marks for the consultant's reasoning (high volume of a standardised product; low unit cost) and two for the constraint created by the other eleven products. A candidate who says only 'flow production is cheaper' has not explained why it would be suitable and earns one mark.

(b) Award (A1) for the mean and (M1)(A1) for the peak monthly demand. The peak is the discriminating figure: a candidate who divides 48 000 by 12 and uses 4 000 as the monthly requirement has not understood the seasonality. Award (M1)(A1) for the batch unit cost and (A1) for the flow unit cost. The comment must note that flow is cheaper on unit cost alone and identify the crossover, but that the comparison ignores capacity.

(c) Award (M1)(A1) for the pre-build quantity of 14 400 benches and the storage cost of EUR 172 800; a candidate who omits the storage cost cannot earn the evaluation marks, because that omission is exactly the error the question is testing. Award the decision-tree marks for the two expected costs. A candidate who computes the expected costs without the storage cost will obtain EUR 888 000 for flow against EUR 924 600 for batch and conclude, wrongly, that flow is cheaper; award the method marks but not the evaluation marks, and credit the candidate if they notice the capacity constraint in words even without the full calculation. Credit any supported conclusion.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the obvious quantitative answer is the wrong one. At 48 000 units a year the flow line costs EUR 20 a bench against EUR 22 for batch, a saving of EUR 96 000, and the crossover point of 36 364 benches is comfortably below the annual volume. On that arithmetic the investment looks clearly worthwhile. The mistake is to compare costs at an annual volume when the constraint binds monthly.

The lever is that the correct operations method is determined by the volume per production run, not by the annual average. The bench sells 48 000 units a year - 4 000 a month on average - but 80% of that volume is sold in three months, so the peak month requires 12 800 benches and the flow line can make 8 000. The shortfall of 4 800 a month must be produced in advance and stored. Storage of 14 400 benches at EUR 3 a bench a month for an average of four months costs EUR 172 800, which is nearly twice the EUR 96 000 saving the flow line creates. The method that is cheapest per unit is not the method that is cheapest to run.

The decision tree reinforces the conclusion and shows that it is robust. Flow is more expensive in both demand states, so the recommendation does not depend on the 0.6 probability. That is a stronger result than a single expected-value calculation would give, and it is worth saying so.

The second constraint - the twelve product variants - is there to show that the arithmetic is not the only obstacle. Flow production is only economic when a line can run without changeover, and Hartswood's range means eleven products would remain on batch. The investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while adding EUR 600 000 of fixed cost.

Classic wrong turns: comparing unit costs at the annual volume and ignoring capacity; dividing annual demand by twelve and using 4 000 as the monthly requirement; computing the decision tree without the storage cost; and concluding that flow must be better because 'higher volume means lower unit cost'.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Unit 5.2 bullet (job, batch and flow production; capital and labour intensity; factors influencing the choice of method), with descriptive statistics and decision trees as the two Toolkit tools. The case was constructed so that flow production is cheaper per unit at the annual volume and at the crossover, while seasonality forces a pre-build whose storage cost exceeds the saving, so that the correct method depends on the volume per run rather than the annual average. The company, the cost structures, the probabilities and every figure are original and were recomputed.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Batch unit cost 180000/48000 + 18.25 = 22.00; flow 480000/48000 + 10 = 20.00; saving 2 x 48000 = 96000; crossover (480000-180000)/(18.25-10) = 36363.6. Mean monthly demand 4000; peak 0.8 x 48000/3 = 12800; shortfall 4800 per month; pre-build 14400; storage 14400 x 3 x 4 = 172800. Batch costs 1056000 and 727500, expected 924600. Flow costs 960000 plus 172800 at high demand and 780000 at low demand, expected 991680; batch lower by 67080. Swept against the HL-only list: no 5.3 lean/quality, 5.6 production planning, 5.7 crisis management, 5.8 R&D or 5.9 management information systems content, and no HL-only Toolkit tool; the Toolkit tools used are descriptive statistics and decision trees only.
